questions.stem: The REGULATING ACT of 1773 was the FIRST step taken by the British Parliament to regulate the affairs of the East India Company. It:

options.option_text: Established the OFFICE OF GOVERNOR-GENERAL of Bengal + a Supreme Court at Calcutta; first = WARREN HASTINGS
Created direct Crown rule over India

questions.explanation: REGULATING ACT OF 1773 — passed by the British Parliament under PM Frederick North to address the corruption + mismanagement of the EIC (East India Company) after the Bengal famine of 1770 + Company's near-bankruptcy. PROVISIONS: (1) Created office of GOVERNOR-GENERAL OF BENGAL (first was WARREN HASTINGS, 1773-1785) with an Executive Council of 4. (2) Governors of Bombay + Madras made SUBORDINATE to GG of Bengal. (3) Established a SUPREME COURT at Calcutta (1774) with a Chief Justice + 3 judges appointed by the Crown — first CJ = Sir Elijah Impey. (4) Prohibited Company servants from private trade or accepting 'presents'. (5) Required Court of Directors to report revenue, civil, military matters to British Govt. LIMITATIONS: (a) GG could be overruled by 3-majority Council; (b) Supreme Court jurisdiction unclear vs Company courts — clashes; (c) PITT's INDIA ACT 1784 (passed by William Pitt the Younger) fixed many of these — established dual control: Court of Directors (commerce) + BOARD OF CONTROL (political affairs, under Crown); GG's council reduced to 3 with decisive vote for GG. SUBSEQUENT Charter Acts (renewing EIC's charter): (1) 1793 — Cornwallis + permanent settlement era. (2) 1813 — ended Company trading monopoly in India (except tea + China trade); allowed missionaries. (3) 1833 — Ended Company's trading activities; GG of Bengal became GG of INDIA (first = William Bentinck); centralised legislation; end of Company's role as traders; Indian Civil Service reformed. (4) 1853 — open competitive examinations for ICS (separated legislative + executive); first ICS exam at London 1855, Indians only from 1864 (Satyendranath Tagore). GOVERNMENT of INDIA ACT 1858 — after 1857 Revolt — ended Company rule, transferred power to British Crown (Queen Victoria), abolished Board of Control + Court of Directors, created Secretary of State for India + Viceroy.

questions.explanation: INDIAN COUNCILS ACT 1909 / MORLEY-MINTO REFORMS — named after the Secretary of State for India (JOHN MORLEY) + Viceroy (LORD MINTO II). BACKGROUND: Partition of Bengal (1905) + Swadeshi agitation + rising Extremist demands. Aims: pacify Moderates, undermine Extremists, divide Hindus + Muslims. KEY PROVISIONS: (1) Enlarged Imperial + Provincial Legislative Councils — INDIANS ADMITTED (limited) for FIRST TIME to ELECTED membership (indirect election via local bodies, landowners, universities). (2) SEPARATE ELECTORATES for MUSLIMS — 'communal' electorates where only Muslims could vote for Muslim candidates; originated from Simla Deputation (1906) by Aga Khan III — led to founding of Muslim League (Dec 1906, Dhaka). (3) SATYENDRA P. SINHA became first INDIAN member of Viceroy's Executive Council; S.P. SINHA + LORD KRISHNA GUPTA also nominated. (4) Indian members could ASK questions + discuss budget — but VOTING power remained advisory. (5) Expanded functions of Legislative Councils — could debate matters of public interest. CRITICISM: (1) Separate electorates = seeds of communalism + eventual Partition; (2) Franchise extremely limited (~1% of population); (3) No transfer of real power; (4) Gokhale welcomed as step; Tilak + Extremists rejected. LALA LAJPAT RAI called Muslim League as 'convenient baby of Minto + Morley'. BEST KNOWN for COMMUNAL ELECTORATES — BAD legacy. Rescinded in part only by Govt of India Act 1935 (joint electorates with reservations). Poll was through Presidency, indirect, with property qualifications. INDIAN COUNCILS ACT 1861 was EARLIER important Act (3 Indians as ADVISORY members only). THE NEXT BIG act was GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms). sowing seeds of future communal politics + two-nation theory.

questions.stem: The GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1919 introduced the system of:
questions.explanation: GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1919 / MONTAGU-CHELMSFORD (Montford) REFORMS — named after Secretary of State EDWIN MONTAGU + Viceroy LORD CHELMSFORD. Introduced following Montagu's DECLARATION of 20 August 1917 — 'gradual development of self-governing institutions + responsible government' was the ULTIMATE aim. KEY FEATURES: (1) DIARCHY in PROVINCES — 'diarchy' = rule by TWO authorities. Provincial subjects SPLIT into: (a) TRANSFERRED (education, public health, agriculture, local govt, industries, etc.) — handled by Indian ministers responsible to Legislative Council; (b) RESERVED (finance, home, law + order, land revenue) — remained with British Governor. Failed experiment — ministers had responsibility without financial power. (2) BICAMERAL CENTRAL Legislature — (a) Council of State (Upper House, 60 members, some elected); (b) Legislative Assembly (Lower House, 145 members, 104 elected). First elected Speaker = Vithalbhai Patel (1925). No real power over Executive though. (3) CENTRAL subject-list + PROVINCIAL list formalised — forerunner to federal structure. (4) SEPARATE ELECTORATES extended to SIKHS, INDIAN CHRISTIANS, ANGLO-INDIANS, EUROPEANS (not just Muslims). (5) Limited franchise based on tax + property; ~7 million voters (out of 300 million population). (6) HIGH COMMISSIONER of INDIA in London established. (7) A STATUTORY commission to report after 10 years — became the SIMON COMMISSION (1927). EVALUATION: (a) Some scope for Indian participation but CORE power retained by British; (b) Congress called it 'inadequate, unsatisfactory + disappointing' (1919 Amritsar session post-Jallianwala); (c) Rowlatt Act + Jallianwala in same year 1919 (April) MADE IT A FARCE in Indian eyes. NEXT Act = Government of India Act 1935 (provincial autonomy, federation), followed by Indian Independence Act 1947. subjects divided into 'TRANSFERRED' (to Indian ministers) + 'RESERVED' (kept with British Governor).

questions.stem: The GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1935 abolished provincial DIARCHY and introduced it at the CENTRE; its PROVINCIAL AUTONOMY feature was enacted but which feature of the Act was never put into force?
questions.explanation: GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1935 — longest British statute enacted on India (451 clauses + 15 Schedules); largely based on (a) Simon Commission Report 1930; (b) Round Table Conferences (1930-32); (c) White Paper 1933 + Joint Select Committee. KEY FEATURES: (1) PROVINCIAL AUTONOMY — provincial diarchy ABOLISHED; entire provincial sphere transferred to elected Indian ministers responsible to Legislative Assembly. Governor remained titular head with 'special responsibilities'. 11 PROVINCES held elections in 1937; Congress formed governments in 7+ provinces; resigned 1939 over WWII without consultation. (2) CENTRAL DIARCHY — introduced at Centre (reverse of 1919 Act provincial diarchy): Executive Council split — DEFENCE, EXTERNAL AFFAIRS, RELIGIOUS AFFAIRS, TRIBES = reserved to Governor-General; rest = transferred to Indian ministers responsible to Federal Legislature. NEVER implemented. (3) ALL-INDIA FEDERATION — envisaged uniting British Provinces + 562 Princely States under one federation. PRINCES had to VOLUNTARILY accede (Instrument of Accession). REFUSED by most Princes (they wanted more power); WWII broke out in Sep 1939 before required number acceded (need 50% of Princely states by population); part never brought into force. (4) BICAMERAL CENTRAL LEGISLATURE (Federal Assembly + Council of States). (5) Separate electorates PRESERVED + EXTENDED (Depressed Classes, women, labour). Poona Pact (1932) compromise on depressed classes. (6) RESERVE BANK OF INDIA (RBI) established 1935 under this Act's powers. (7) FEDERAL COURT (1937) — precursor to Supreme Court; first CJ = Sir Maurice Gwyer. (8) Franchise extended to ~14% (~30 million voters). (9) BURMA separated (1937). SIGNIFICANCE: MOST PROVISIONS of the 1935 Act were ADOPTED into the 1950 INDIAN CONSTITUTION — 'Ambedkar's constitution is essentially a federation modelled on the 1935 Act' — notable inspirations include: federal division of powers, Concurrent List, emergency provisions, public service commissions, federal court structure. never became operational because princes did not accede by 1939/WWII; envisaged joining princely states with British provinces.

questions.stem: The INDIAN INDEPENDENCE ACT 1947 was PASSED by the British Parliament on:
questions.explanation: INDIAN INDEPENDENCE ACT 1947 — passed by British Parliament on 18 JULY 1947 (Royal Assent); implemented based on MOUNTBATTEN PLAN (3 June 1947). PROVISIONS: (1) Partition of BRITISH INDIA into two DOMINIONS — INDIA + PAKISTAN, effective 15 August 1947 (midnight of 14/15). Dominion Status = sovereign + self-governing under British Crown (similar to Canada + Australia). (2) Ended British sovereignty over Indian Princely States — each to accede to either India or Pakistan or remain independent (most acceded via Instruments of Accession; Hyderabad, Junagadh, Jammu + Kashmir were controversial). (3) Office of Secretary of State for India abolished. (4) Britain's MONARCH ceased to use the title 'Emperor of India' (George VI, effective 22 June 1948). (5) Constituent Assemblies of both Dominions to draft new constitutions (Indian CA already existed since Dec 1946). Sir Cyril Radcliffe was given 5 weeks (July-Aug 1947) to demarcate BOUNDARIES between India + Pakistan (West = Punjab; East = Bengal) — RADCLIFFE LINE; published 17 Aug 1947 (2 days after independence); caused massive displacement + ~15 million refugees + estimated 1-2 million deaths in Partition violence. LEADING UP TO IT: (a) CRIPPS MISSION (1942) — rejected (offered dominion status + constitution-making body after war); (b) QUIT INDIA (Aug 1942); (c) WAVELL PLAN / SIMLA CONF (1945) — failed over Muslim League's demand for exclusive Muslim representation; (d) CABINET MISSION (1946) — rejected; (e) DIRECT ACTION DAY (16 Aug 1946, Jinnah) → Great Calcutta Killings; (f) Mountbatten appointed March 1947; (g) 3 June Plan announced partition. JINNAH became Pakistan's 1st Governor-General (Aug 1947 - Sep 1948 died); Mountbatten was India's 1st Governor-General (till June 1948, succeeded by C. Rajagopalachari — only + last Indian GG). Nehru became 1st PM; Constitution came into force 26 Jan 1950 — making India a REPUBLIC. received Royal Assent; partitioned British India into DOMINIONS of India + Pakistan on 15 August 1947.

questions.stem: 'DIVIDE + RULE' policy was deepened by the COMMUNAL AWARD (1932) announced by British PM:
questions.explanation: COMMUNAL AWARD — announced on 16 August 1932 by British PM RAMSAY MacDONALD (Labour Party, National Government) to resolve the communal representation question at the 2nd Round Table Conference in London where Indian parties had failed to agree. PROVISIONS: SEPARATE ELECTORATES for (a) Muslims (expanded since 1909); (b) Sikhs; (c) Indian Christians; (d) Anglo-Indians; (e) Europeans; AND additionally now for (f) DEPRESSED CLASSES (SCs/Dalits); (g) Women. B.R. AMBEDKAR (at the RTC) had argued for separate electorates for Dalits to ensure their political representation independent of caste-Hindus. GANDHI bitterly opposed — believed separate Dalit electorate would permanently divide Hindu society + postpone social reform. GANDHI'S FAST-UNTO-DEATH (20 September 1932) at YERAVADA JAIL, Pune — where he was imprisoned during Civil Disobedience. Gandhi's death fear sparked nationwide agitation. POONA PACT (24 September 1932, signed by Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya on behalf of Hindus + AMBEDKAR for the depressed classes) — compromise: (a) SINGLE general electorate for Hindus (no separate Dalit electorate); (b) but RESERVED SEATS for Dalits — 148 (up from 78 in the Communal Award) within general constituencies; (c) primary election among Dalits to select 4 candidates, then general electorate chose 1; (d) LOCAL bodies + govt services promises for Dalits. INDIAN Constitution (1950) preserved the spirit — joint electorates + reserved seats for SC + ST in Lok Sabha + State Assemblies (originally 10-year sunset, renewed every 10 years, latest 104th CAA 2020 extended to 2030). Separate electorates for religious minorities were ABOLISHED in Constitution. Ambedkar's legacy: Constitution's architect; Father of Indian Constitution; Bharat Ratna (posthumous 1990). extended separate electorates to 'DEPRESSED CLASSES' (Dalits); Gandhi opposed with fast-unto-death; POONA PACT (1932) with Ambedkar compromised.

questions.stem: Which Viceroy is associated with the introduction of 'LOCAL SELF-GOVERNMENT' in India (1882) and is called the 'FATHER OF LOCAL SELF-GOVERNMENT'?
questions.explanation: LORD RIPON (George Frederick Samuel Robinson; Viceroy 1880-1884) — reformist Liberal Viceroy appointed by Gladstone's government. Known as 'FATHER OF LOCAL SELF-GOVERNMENT IN INDIA'. KEY REFORMS: (1) RIPON'S RESOLUTION of 18 MAY 1882 — on 'Local Self-Government' — decentralisation of municipal administration; majority of members to be ELECTED NON-OFFICIALS; limited governmental control; local institutions = 'political + popular education'. Led to creation of elected municipal bodies, district boards, local funds in various provinces. (2) HUNTER COMMISSION on EDUCATION (1882) — first major review after Wood's Despatch 1854; recommended primary education in mother-tongue, expansion of govt-aided schools, promotion of women's + vocational education. (3) REPEAL of VERNACULAR PRESS ACT (1882) — Lord Lytton had passed the repressive Act 1878 targeting Indian-language press; Ripon repealed it restoring press freedom. (4) ILBERT BILL (1883) — proposed by law-member Courtenay Ilbert — would allow INDIAN judges to try EUROPEANS in mofussil courts (no racial distinction). CAUSED UPROAR among British residents + press ('white revolt') against it; forced Ripon to DILUTE it (1884) — final compromise: Indian judges could try Europeans only with a jury of Europeans (majority). The episode exposed RACIAL ARROGANCE of British in India + taught Indians power of organised political agitation — influenced the founding of INC in 1885. (5) FACTORIES ACT 1881 (enacted, Ripon oversaw implementation) — first factory legislation, restricted child labour. LEGACY: Ripon remains probably the ONLY Viceroy genuinely LIKED by Indians. Ripon Club in Bombay, Ripon College in Kolkata (now Surendranath College) named after him. Nationalists gave him a hero's farewell when he left India. OPPOSITE to him — LORD LYTTON (Viceroy 1876-80): Vernacular Press Act 1878, Arms Act 1878, Delhi Durbar 1877 (proclaimed Queen Victoria as Empress of India), stoked second Afghan War, Great Famine 1876-78 (5M deaths). liberal Viceroy; Ripon's Resolution 1882 introduced elected municipal bodies, laid foundation for modern local self-government.

questions.stem: The SIMON COMMISSION (1927-1930), which came to India to review the 1919 Act, was boycotted because:
questions.explanation: SIMON COMMISSION — 7-member STATUTORY Commission appointed in Nov 1927 (3 years early, because Tory Conservative govt wanted to pre-empt incoming Labour from appointing liberal Indian members). OFFICIAL TITLE: Indian Statutory Commission. CHAIR: SIR JOHN SIMON. Purpose: review the working of the Government of India Act 1919 + recommend constitutional reforms. ALL-WHITE composition (7 British MPs including CLEMENT ATTLEE — future PM who granted Indian independence 1947) → SEEN AS AN INSULT to Indian aspirations. NATIONWIDE BOYCOTT: (1) CONGRESS (Madras Session Dec 1927, Ansari) resolved to boycott. (2) Muslim League (Jinnah) boycotted. (3) ARRIVED IN BOMBAY on 3 FEBRUARY 1928 — massive protests. Black flags + slogan 'SIMON GO BACK'. (4) LAHORE protest on 30 OCTOBER 1928 — LALA LAJPAT RAI ('Lion of Punjab') led 'Simon Go Back' procession. Superintendent JAMES SCOTT ordered lathi charge; Lajpat Rai severely injured + died on 17 NOV 1928 (apparently from injuries + heart attack). His last words: 'every blow inflicted on me is a nail in the coffin of the British Empire'. REVENGE: HSRA (Bhagat Singh + Rajguru + Chandra Shekhar Azad) killed (by mistake) ASP J.P. SAUNDERS on 17 Dec 1928 (mistaken for Scott). Saunders murder → Lahore Conspiracy Case → Bhagat Singh + Sukhdev + Rajguru hanged 23 March 1931. NEHRU REPORT (1928) — response by All Parties Conference, drafted by MOTILAL NEHRU — India's first attempt at constitutional self-drafting; demanded DOMINION STATUS, joint electorates, fundamental rights; rejected by Jinnah (who submitted 14-point demand including separate electorates). SIMON REPORT (May 1930, 2 vols) — recommended abolition of diarchy, provincial autonomy, federation, continued communal electorates — basis for Govt of India Act 1935. Meanwhile Round Table Conferences (1930-32) ran in parallel. Attlee's exposure to India during this Commission likely influenced his 1947 decision to grant independence. all 7 British members; greeted with 'SIMON GO BACK' protests; Lala Lajpat Rai died after lathi-charge (Nov 1928).

questions.stem: The PERMANENT SETTLEMENT of BENGAL (1793), fixing land revenue in PERPETUITY with Zamindars, was introduced by Governor-General:
questions.explanation: LORD CORNWALLIS — Governor-General of Bengal 1786-1793 (returned briefly 1805 + died). Before India, he was the British general who SURRENDERED to George Washington at YORKTOWN (1781) ending the American Revolutionary War — a post-Yorktown 'rehabilitation' posting in India. KEY REFORMS: (1) PERMANENT SETTLEMENT of Bengal (1793) — fixed land revenue demand in PERPETUITY from ZAMINDARS (landlords, mainly Hindu); revenue = 10/11 of rental; zamindars could keep 1/11. Created private PROPERTY in land; zamindars became owners. Applied in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, parts of Madras + UP (~19% of British India). RYOTWARI SYSTEM (direct revenue from cultivators, no intermediary) elsewhere — introduced by Munro in Madras 1820 + later Bombay. MAHALWARI system — village-level revenue. CORNWALLIS CODE 1793 = 48 regulations — established fundamentals of civil + criminal admin. (2) FATHER of CIVIL SERVICE IN INDIA — separated revenue + judicial services; created COVENANTED Service (higher ranks, British only); reformed police + judiciary; abolished Nizamat Adalats. Introduced hierarchy of courts — munsiff, district court, provincial court, Sadar Diwani Adalat, Sadar Nizamat Adalat. Brought district collectors + magistrates. (3) POLICING reforms — district superintendents, thanas, officers' accountability. ASSESSMENT: (1) Permanent settlement BENEFITED zamindars hugely + gave stable revenue to British; BUT failed cultivators (rents passed on + exploited) + led to SUB-INFEUDATION + absentee landlordism; (2) reduced opportunity cost for British administrators + made governance professional; (3) 1793 code was a foundation of Indian jurisprudence. Cornwallis died at GHAZIPUR (UP, 1805) on a second stint + is buried there. SUCCESSOR: LORD WELLESLEY (GG 1798-1805) — SUBSIDIARY ALLIANCE system, Mysore wars (defeated Tipu 1799), Maratha wars. introduced Zamindari system in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha; FATHER of CIVIL SERVICE IN INDIA; GG 1786-93, 1805.

questions.stem: The WOOD'S DESPATCH of 1854 is known as the 'MAGNA CARTA' of:
questions.explanation: WOOD'S DESPATCH of 1854 — drafted by SIR CHARLES WOOD, President of Board of Control of EIC — sent to Governor-General Lord DALHOUSIE as a policy directive on Education. Hence 'DESPATCH'. Known as 'MAGNA CARTA of English Education in India' or 'MAGNA CARTA of INDIAN EDUCATION'. KEY PROVISIONS: (1) COMPREHENSIVE education system — from primary (vernacular-medium) → high school (Anglo-vernacular) → UNIVERSITY (English-medium) — three-tier pyramid. (2) Establishment of UNIVERSITIES at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras — founded 1857 on the University of London model (examining, not teaching — affiliated colleges, central examinations). (3) Creation of DEPARTMENTS OF PUBLIC INSTRUCTION in 5 provinces (Bengal, NWFP, Bombay, Madras, Punjab); designated Director of Public Instruction. (4) GRANTS-IN-AID system for private schools + colleges; fostered Christian missionary + Indian educational enterprise. (5) STRESS on Women's education — 'Girls' schools need encouragement'. (6) Promoted VERNACULAR languages (mother-tongue) for mass education (unusual for colonial Britain — but practical). (7) VOCATIONAL + TECHNICAL education encouraged — engineering colleges (Roorkee 1847), law colleges. EARLIER ORIENTALIST vs ANGLICIST DEBATE (1820s-30s): (a) Orientalists (H.H. Wilson etc.) — promote Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian education; (b) ANGLICISTS (T.B. MACAULAY, Minute on Indian Education 1835) — 'English at the apex' → produce a 'class Indian in blood + colour, English in tastes + opinions, intellect + morals'. MACAULAY'S MINUTE (1835) won; Bentinck's Resolution March 1835 adopted ENGLISH as medium of higher education + GOV language. INSTITUTIONS: (1) Fort William College (1800, for Company servants). (2) Hindu College Calcutta 1817 (first modern Indian college, founded by Raja Rammohan Roy + David Hare). (3) ELPHINSTONE COLLEGE Bombay 1834. (4) Calcutta Medical College 1835, Grant Medical College Bombay 1845. OTHER education commissions: HUNTER 1882 (Ripon); RALEIGH 1902 (Curzon); SADLER 1917; HARTOG 1929; WARDHA 1937 (Gandhi-Zakir Hussain basic education scheme). Post-independence: RADHAKRISHNAN 1948 (universities); KOTHARI 1964-66 (comprehensive); NEP 1968, 1986, 2020. laid framework for modern Indian education system; established universities at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857).
